articles.title: Examining associations between brain volume and alexithymia in autistic youth and young adults
articles.authors: Goldie McQuaid; Gregory Wallace; Alex Job Said; Stefen Beeler-Duden; Zachary Jacokes; Kevin Pelphrey; Allison Jack
articles.abstract:
Alexithymia is a dimensional trait including challenges labeling emotions. Alexithymia is elevated in autistic individuals relative to the general population and is suggested to be part of the broader autism phenotype. Alexithymia is also independently associated with emotion regulation challenges, which are more prevalent among autistic persons, and with two of the most common co-occurring conditions among autistic people: depression and anxiety. A better understanding of alexithymia, including its neural correlates, therefore promises to advance our understanding of risk profiles for mental health problems in autistic people.

We therefore sought to: 1) characterize alexithymia in autistic (n=54) and neurotypical (n=56) adolescents and young adults (15-25y) including group and sex differences; 2) examine group and sex differences in brain volume in eight regions of interest implicated in alexithymia; and 3) explore potential interactions between group and brain volume as predictors of alexithymia.

Autistic individuals self-reported significantly higher levels of alexithymia relative to neurotypical individuals, with autistic females reporting the highest levels and neurotypical males the lowest levels. There were no differences in group or sex based on brain volume. Exploratory models predicting alexithymia found a significant interaction between group and right dorsal anterior cingulate cortex volume.

articles.title: “What’s our color? POOR”: Exploring the Consequences of Racism-Conscious Framings of Environmental Exposures
articles.authors: Harrison James Schmitt; Lily Schwartzman; Trevor Scott Lies
articles.abstract: Environmental justice activists increasingly pursue public awareness campaigns to garner support as they face injustice. However, little psychological research has investigated the implications of different framings of recognition justice for collective action. Two experiments with qualitative components test the primary hypothesis that recognition of systemic racism in environmental exposures may represent a double-edged sword. We test implications of racism-conscious framings of inequitable lead exposures on collective action intentions among Black, Latine, and White US residents. Study 1 (n=590) finds that a racism-conscious frame increases anger and systemic knowledge of racism but does not affect collective action intentions, except among highly racially identified White participants, whose collective action intentions decreased after the manipulation. Results of Study 2 (n=703) suggest that a combined racism- and class-conscious frame may prevent (highly-identified) White disengagement from collective action. We discuss addressing environmental injustice through coalition building while acknowledging the double-edged sword of racism-conscious recognition.

articles.title: A Dyadic Perspective on Reactive Aggression: Temporal Behavioral and Neural Dynamics in Sibling Interactions
articles.authors: Julia Koch; Lucia Hernandez-Pena; Dorothea M.G. König; Julia Schräder; Katja Bertsch; Andreas Meyer-Lindenberg; Edward S. Brodkin; Ute Habel; Rik Sijben; Lisa Wagels
articles.abstract: Aggression contributes to interpersonal conflict and societal harm. Although aggressive behavior unfolds within social interactions, it has largely been studied as an individual process. Siblings offer dyadic contexts in which aggression is shaped by developmental and relational dynamics. Here, we investigated how aggressive behavior and its neural correlates unfold dynamically within and across healthy adult siblings. Ninety-four siblings from 47 dyads completed an interactive version of the Taylor Aggression Paradigm (iTAP) during simultaneous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). We applied actor-partner interdependence models to predict each sibling’s neural activity during aggressive decision-making from both siblings’ neural responses during the preceding provocation feedback phase and tested whether these associations depended on relationship engagement, as measured by the Sibling Type Questionnaire (STQ) Mutuality subscale. Behaviorally, individuals’ subsequent responses were predicted by their own and their sibling’s preceding behavior. In parallel, greater ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) activity during provocation feedback was associated with greater subsequent amygdala activity during aggressive decision-making within and across siblings, whereas lower dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) activity in one sibling was associated with greater subsequent amygdala activity in the other. Relationship engagement strengthened the actor vmPFC-amygdala association and moderated the partner vmPFC-amygdala association. Exploratory analyses linked dmPFC activity during provocation to participants’ previous aggressive decisions, but not subsequent aggression. Together, these findings show that aggression is embedded in temporally structured behavioral and neural dynamics involving both interaction partners, implicating medial prefrontal regulatory systems in dyadic interaction and highlighting the importance of interpersonal reciprocity and relationship history for understanding aggression.

articles.title: Gender comes first: Experimental evidence for the representation of gender closer to the noun stem than number across linguistic populations
articles.authors: Carmen Saldana; Patrick Njue Kanampiu; Jennifer Culbertson
articles.abstract: Morphosyntactic expression exhibits significant cross-linguistic variation, yet systematic tendencies emerge. Gender and number features are frequently co-expressed within a single exponent, and when realised separately, gender morphology tends to surface closer to the stem. Competing theoretical accounts of gender and number seek to explain these tendencies, but empirical validation remains challenging due to sparse typological data. Across a series of artificial language learning experiments, we demonstrate that learners exhibit a robust preference for placing nominal morphology encoding gender information closest to the stem. This bias, consistent across English, Italian, and Kîîtharaka speakers, holds both for prefixing and suffixing morphology, and across different types of gender and number systems.These results provide a new source of empirical support for theories proposing a gender-first derivation and highlights cognitive constraints influencing morpheme order.

articles.title: Do Scales Semantically Resemble the Sources They Cite? Embedding Analysis of Construct Proliferation in Five Anomy Instruments
articles.authors: Mateo Belalcazar; Joan Sebastian Diaz Mona; Nelson Molina Valencia; Yenny Otálora
articles.abstract:
Construct proliferation in psychology is associated with jingle and jangle fallacies that psychometric methods are not designed to detect. Semantic embeddings offer a complementary approach, but existing applications have compared scales within a single level without bringing in the theoretical texts a construct's tradition rests on. This study extends the embedding framework of Wulff and Mata (2025a) to a
cross-level comparison paired with a documentary audit of citation acts. We embedded 43 items from five anomy scales alongside 3,762 propositions extracted from nine source texts at three analytical levels (foundational texts, scale articles, and items), using six embedding models from three architectural families, and we coded every passage in which a scale article cites a theoretical source. Items formed
  thematic clusters that crossed scale boundaries, beyond the expression of a single homogeneous theme per instrument, while retaining within-scale cohesion, and were rarely nearest to the article that introduced them (14%). All five scale articles were semantically nearest to Merton's (1938) text, a pattern identical across models, stable under bootstrap resampling, and not reproduced by two genre-matched control texts. The documentary audit showed that no article adopts Merton's formulation; the two articles that adopt a foundational text both adopt Durkheim's Suicide, which was the nearest foundation for neither of them. This proximity coexists with the absence of any direct adoption of Merton. This extension, combining semantic proximity with documented citation acts, offers an approach for examining whether the sources an instrument cites are also the ones its content most resembles.

articles.title: Motivational Framing Shapes Effort Judgments in Individuals with Depressive Symptoms
articles.authors: Thomas Meyer; Rebecca Kochtokrax; Hannah Sautmann; Nexhmedin Morina
articles.abstract: Effort-related motivational deficits in depression are often studied through effort-reward decisions, yet everyday effort also depends on the reference standards against which it is judged. In a preregistered laboratory crossover study, 51 participants with at least mild depressive symptoms received two opposing effort framings: self-initiated allocation toward goals and need frustration emphasizing burden and affective demand. After reconstructing previous-day activities, participants evaluated upward and downward social, temporal-past, criteria-based, and counterfactual standards for their two most effortful activities per session, yielding 1,632 standard-endorsement judgments followed by intensity and discrepancy ratings for endorsed standards. As predicted, need-frustration framing increased endorsement of upward criteria-based standards (“this should feel less effortful”). However, this effect did not generalize across upward comparisons. Instead, need frustration decreased upward temporal standards (“this used to feel easier”) and increased downward counterfactual standards (“it could have been harder under worse circumstances”). Intensity ratings among endorsed standards were not reliably affected, although an exploratory relevance score supported the specific role of upward criteria-based standards. Perceived effort was higher under allocation but correlated more positively with depressive symptoms under need frustration. These findings suggest that motivational framing changes the comparison standards people identify as relevant to everyday effort judgments and highlight the need to assess the appraised meaning of effort-related comparisons directly.

articles.title: Language at Scale: Functional Informational Interchangeability and the Child–LLM Data Gap
articles.authors: Yonata Levy
articles.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable linguistic competence through exposure to
far more language than children ever encounter. We examine whether this Child–LLM data gap
rests on an incomplete comparison of the information available to children. Drawing on language
acquisition research and information theory, we propose Functional Informational
Interchangeability: extensive linguistic input can supply models with information that is
interchangeable with the information children obtain through combined linguistic, perceptual,
motor, emotional and social experiences. Relevance, redundancy, joint information and learnerdependent uptake provide tools for testing this hypothesis. The proposal reframes the Child–
LLM data gap around information relevant to acquiring linguistic knowledge. If the
contributions of these environments prove comparable in task-relevant informational units, the
apparent gap may disappear.

articles.title: The Other Side of Prolific: Ethical Research Guidelines Based on a Mixed Methods Investigation of Prolific Platform Workers’ Experiences
articles.authors: Louis Bachaud; Macken Murphy; Antoine Marie
articles.abstract:
Experimental and survey research is increasingly reliant on crowdsourced
participant recruitment platforms like Prolific. Yet, while Prolific workers are arguably one of the
most well-studied populations in human history, little is known about their actual working
conditions. This preregistered mixed-methods study explores working conditions on Prolific
drawing on different sources: (1) a qualitative inductive analysis of the r/ProlificAC subreddit, a
platform where Prolific workers gather to discuss their experiences; (2) statistics from a survey on
working conditions, labor identity, income, motivations, fraud, and potential grievances of Prolific
workers (n=455); (3) qualitative analyses of open-ended responses to the same survey. Overall,
these analyses reveal an unbalanced power dynamic on the platform, with the workers at a
disadvantage relative to researchers, due to competition between workers, lack of social protection,
hurdles to collective organization, and platform design—logics inherent to the crowdsourcing
model. We also reveal for the first time clear evidence of fraud on the worker side of Prolific,
through a secondary market of trading and faking accounts. Based on these findings, we provide
clear and actionable guidelines for researchers wishing to use the platform in an ethical way. We
also suggest steps for the Prolific company to both ensure data quality and guarantee fair relations
between clients and workers.

articles.title: Convincing Without Conflict? Persuasion and Its Social Costs in Human–AI Conversations About Meat Reduction
articles.authors: Elena Wurth; Georg Ahnert; Ira Elisa Herwig; Ahmed Salem; Markus Strohmaier; Jutta Mata
articles.abstract: Meat consumption in high-income countries exceeds recommendations. Because meals are often shared, conversations can spark meat reduction, yet advocates often remain silent because persuading carries social costs. Generative AI has proven persuasive and could inform such conversations. Drawing on research on persuasion and reactance, we examined how persuasion and its social costs depend on the source of the strategies and on the medium delivering them. In a preregistered 5 × 2 experiment (N = 521), participants discussed a shared meal with a fictional counterpart, either a chatbot or a text-based script. The counterpart used strategies from the behavioral science literature, a large language model, or a generative agent simulation, or did not argue for meat reduction (neutral and placebo controls). Arguing for meat reduction increased intentions and more than quadrupled the odds of choosing a vegetarian dish in both media; arguing for an unrelated sustainability behavior did not shift choice. Persuasion increased perceived threat to freedom but did not reduce liking of the counterpart. AI-derived strategies persuaded as well as literature-based strategies, at no higher social cost. As predicted, the chatbot incurred higher social costs than the text-based dialogue. Studies of AI-based persuasion should assess social costs alongside persuasiveness.

articles.title: Dynamic resource allocation in temporal working memory: interplay of decay, interference and attention
articles.authors: Yunyun Shen; Sophie K Herbst; Virginie van Wassenhove
articles.abstract: How does a moment become a memory trace? The transition from perceived duration to the when of memory is likely shaped by attention and working memory (WM). In two experiments, we investigated how memory decay, interference between stored durations, and internal versus external attention affect the precision of recall from temporal WM. For this, we used a delayed reproduction task in which participants listened to a sequence of time intervals and reproduced them after a retention period (Herbst et al., 2025). In Experiment 1, we manipulated the ratio between the target interval and the retention interval, showing that both the duration of the retention interval (decay) and its ratio to the target (temporal distinctiveness yielding interference) affected WM performance. In Experiment 2, we examined interference between intervals within a sequence by manipulating attention via a cue indicating which interval to reproduce. The cue appeared either before (pro-cue) or after (retro-cue) the retention period, directing external attention to sensory encoding or internal attention to WM representations, respectively, either for a single item or the full sequence. External attention selectively benefited accuracy and precision for the longest item when cued alone in the final position. Retro-cueing, by contrast, more generally reduced precision for single-item compared to the whole-sequence recall. Finally, a mixture modeling approach revealed swap errors consistent with those observed in visual WM. Together, these findings compare the contributions of decay and temporal distinctiveness to temporal WM performance with a dynamic resource allocation framework.

articles.title: AI versus human source attribution and perceived empathy in supportive communication: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles.authors: Arthur Bran Herbener; Filip Skjold Thidemann; Caroline Gjørtsvang Kock; Malene Flensborg Damholdt
articles.abstract: Research suggests that people attribute less empathy to supportive communication labelled as AI-generated rather than human-written, but the evidence is mixed, and it is unclear whether the effect varies with how empathy is conceptualized and operationalized. In the present paper, we report a systematic review and meta-analysis of source-attribution effects (human vs. AI) on perceived empathy in supportive communication. A systematic literature search identified 10 records reporting the results of 18 independent studies (N = 13,541). We observed a small source-attribution effect on perceived general empathy (g = 0.41, 95% CI [0.23, 0.58]), cognitive empathy (g = 0.39, 95% CI [0.16, 0.63]), motivational empathy (g = 0.42, 95% CI [0.19, 0.64]), and a moderate effect for affective empathy (g = 0.50, 95% CI [0.19, 0.81]). However, substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies. Alt-hough gender initially emerged as a significant moderator of general perceived empathy, this association was no longer significant after excluding two influential outliers. The analyses also found no statistically significant moderation by age, exposure type (vignette vs. first-person interaction), or supportive setting. Thus, the sources of the substantial between-study heterogeneity remain largely unex-plained. Future research is needed to identify the conditions shaping source-attribution effects on empathy and evaluate whether these effects persist or fade over the course of interactions.

articles.title: Feasibility of virtual reality in assessing functional communication in persons with aphasia
articles.authors: Marina Ruiter; Vitória Piai; Hilde Bosschers; Mirjam Otters; Lizet van Ewijk; Edward Bosma; Willemijn Josefien Doedens
articles.abstract: Functional communication skills represent important measures in aphasia therapy. Assessing these skills, however, remains challenging. Mainstream pen-and-paper based instruments often elicit indirect rather than direct speech and fail to capture the complex communicative demands encountered in everyday communication situations, limiting their ecological validity and construct validity. The current study explored the feasibility of using immersive Virtual Reality (iVR) to assess functional communication in persons with aphasia. After developing a proof-of-concept version – incorporating the needs and ideas of both speech and language therapists and persons with aphasia - we investigated whether (1) iVR enables a realistic simulation of everyday communication, including its technical feasibility and acceptability for the intended users, and (2)  iVR simulation has added value for functional communication assessment by allowing manipulation of communicative complexity, the elicitation of direct speech, and both verbal and non-verbal aspects of communication to be assessed. The results suggest that it is technically feasible to create iVR environments for the assessment of functional communication in persons with aphasia that are acceptable to (end) users and that enhance the construct validity of functional communication tests. Despite remaining areas for improvement, iVR was found to have a clear added value for assessment purposes.

articles.title: Risks and Benefits of Neuroticism in Adolescence: Longitudinal Evidence from Population and Clinic-Referred Samples
articles.authors: Larissa Lucia Wieczorek; Eva Bleckmann; Solomiia Myroniuk; Bertus F. Jeronimus; Sanne Booij; Jenny Wagner; Albertine Oldehinkel
articles.abstract:
Background: Neuroticism is known for being linked to detrimental outcomes, but it may also serve beneficial functions in adolescence, where avoiding and protecting oneself from risks becomes crucial. 
Method: We examined potential risks and benefits of neuroticism based on longitudinal data of two samples of Dutch adolescents, one population (n = 2229, 51% female) and one clinic-referred (n = 543, 34% female) sample. Neuroticism was measured with parent-ratings of the temperament facets fear and frustration and used to predict a diverse set of outcomes in the domains lifestyle choices (e.g., substance abuse) and social resources (e.g., social skills) between ages 11 to 19. 
Results: High neuroticism conveyed heightened risk but three key observations refine this picture: (1) fear related to fewer risks than frustration and was additionally linked to benefits regarding better social skills and more prosocial behavior among adolescents in the clinic-referred sample; (2) both fear and frustration were consistently associated with parent-rated social behavior problems across measurement points, while other risk-related associations were less consistent; (3) most links between fear and detrimental outcomes became non-significant after controlling for childhood adversity (e.g., low socioeconomic status, parental divorce). 
Conclusions: Although our results indicate several risk-related effects, we also provide initial evidence that the fear facet of neuroticism can be beneficial in adolescence, especially among youth with a clinical background and in the social domain. We call for more nuanced research studying the potential protective role of neuroticism within high-risk populations.

articles.title: Momentary Emotion Differentiation:  A Theory-Consistent Index that is Disambiguated from Momentary Affect
articles.authors: Yiqin Zhu; Matthew H. S. Ng; Richard Morris; Renee J Thompson
articles.abstract: Emotion differentiation (ED), the ability to distinguish among one’s emotional experiences, has been increasingly studied as a momentary process. Extending ED measurement in this way raises questions about what a momentary ED index should capture and how it should relate to momentary affect and perceived sources of emotion. We derived a divergence-based index and compared it with an existing sum-based ED index in two ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies. College students (Sample 1; N = 268) and community adults (Sample 2; N = 179) reported emotions five times a day for 12 or 14 days, respectively. Individuals in Sample 1 also reported perceived source and fit of emotions. Divergence-based ED captures how emotion ratings depart from one another, while sum-based ED captures shared shifts across ratings. Across samples, both indices, when aggregated, yielded the same rank ordering as trait-level ED, and showed substantial within-person fluctuations. Divergence-based ED retained most of its within-person variance after adjusting for momentary affect or squared affect, while sum-based ED retained little after adjusting for squared affect. In Sample 1, greater-than-usual clarity about the source of feelings and better-than-usual fit between feelings and the situations were associated with higher divergence-based ED and lower sum-based ED. Simulations identified conditions under which response-scale endpoints can produce artifactual associations between divergence-based ED and momentary affect. Findings support appropriate use of divergence-based ED, especially as an outcome when momentary affect needs to be considered. We provide design and analysis recommendations and R code for applying divergence-based ED to EMA datasets.

articles.title: Feeling Good Sustains Acting Green: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Warm Glow and Pro-Environmental Behavior
articles.authors: Linli Zhou; Cameron Brick; Disa Sauter
articles.abstract: When we engage in pro-environmental behaviors that align with our personal values, we can experience positive feelings, known as warm glow. Theories suggest a potential positive feedback loop such that people who anticipate feeling more warm glow are more likely to act pro-environmentally, and acting in line with their personal values may in turn elicit warm glow, thereby encouraging further pro-environmental behavior. There is considerable empirical work from psychology, marketing and economics investigating these relationships, but to date this work has not been systematically synthesized. A test of the strength and robustness of the theorized links is needed to answer the question of whether warm glow is in fact consistently related to pro-environmental behavior. We report a systematic review and meta-analysis probing the robustness of the associations between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Following the PRISMA guidance, we identified 94 papers with 251 effects based on 58,313 participants. A pre-registered three-level random-effects meta-analytic model was used to estimate overall effects and to examine moderation by behavioral domain and measurement approach. The associations between both anticipated and experienced warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors were robust and medium-to-large (rs: .43 – .53). Substantial heterogeneity persisted after accounting for moderators, suggesting meaningful variation in effect sizes across studies. Overall, these findings provide strong evidence of robust links between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Future research using experimental and longitudinal designs is needed to help test the causal pathways in the positive feedback loop.

articles.title: What Do Global Life Evaluations Capture?
articles.authors: Irene Johanna Elisabeth Teulings; Espen Røysamb; Ludvig Daae Bjørndal; Esten Høyland Leonardsen; Ragnhild Bang Nes; Jinrui Liu; Matthew Iasiello; Joar Vittersø
articles.abstract: Life satisfaction is widely used as a primary indicator of population wellbeing in research and policymaking. Yet it remains unclear which wellbeing domains contribute to life satisfaction and other global life evaluations. In a UK sample (N = 1,050), we examined how four global measures (Satisfaction With Life Scale, single-item life satisfaction, Cantril’s Ladder, a good life evaluation) reflected experiences across 15 wellbeing domains. Machine learning analyses identified optimism, personal circumstances, happiness, and meaning and purpose as the strongest predictors, with other domains contributing little predictive information. Crucially, domains’ contributions corresponded only weakly with participants’ domain importance ratings, challenging the assumption that unequal contributions of domains reflect what people value most. Global life evaluations thus appear to provide selectively weighted rather than comprehensive summaries of wellbeing, potentially underrepresenting certain domains people consider important. Researchers and policymakers seeking comprehensive or value-based assessments could therefore complement global measures with multidimensional assessments.

articles.title: Development of a Two-Dimensional Boredom Intolerance Scale and Associations Between Boredom Intolerance and Problematic Short-Video Use
articles.authors: Zhifang Hu; YueLin; Qinxue Liu
articles.abstract:
With digital applications becoming increasingly integrated into daily life, individuals may become less tolerant of boredom. However, existing measures of boredom intolerance have primarily focused on negative emotional responses to boredom, while providing limited insight into behavioral tendencies when encountering boredom. The present study developed a two-dimensional Boredom Intolerance Scale through five studies and examined the associations between boredom intolerance and problematic short-video use.
Study 1 used qualitative interviews and grounded theory analysis to identify the conceptual domains and dimensions of boredom intolerance, revealing two dimensions: emotional intolerance and behavioral avoidance. Study 2 conducted exploratory factor analysis with 444 participants (Mage = 23.99 ± 5.41 years; 66.89% female) and developed an eight-item two-dimensional scale. Study 3 conducted confirmatory factor analysis and criterion-related validity analyses with 347 participants (Mage = 21.79 ± 3.38 years; 74.64% female), further supporting the two-dimensional structure of boredom intolerance. Study 4 employed a two-wave longitudinal design with 219 participants (Mage = 21.62 ± 2.56 years; 78.5% female) and found that problematic short-video use positively predicted boredom intolerance. Study 5 used a 14-day diary design with 185 participants (Mage = 21.13 ± 1.54 years; 85.4% female) and found that boredom intolerance positively predicted state-level problematic short-video use.

articles.title: Mitigating Retest Effects in High-Frequency Cognitive Assessment Data: A Tutorial on the Bayesian Double Exponential Model in Stan
articles.authors: Yanling Li; Joachim Vandekerckhove; Grace J. Chen; Martin Sliwinski; Zita Oravecz
articles.abstract: In this tutorial, we give a comprehensive, step-by-step guide for implementing the Bayesian Double Exponential Model (BDEM) in the popular Bayesian software Stan. The BDEM is a statistical tool designed to disentangle retest effects from true longitudinal cognitive change and to quantify individual differences in high-frequency repeated cognitive assessment data, typically collected in everyday settings. We give step-by-step guidelines for fitting BDEM in Stan and also describe implementations in PyMC and JAGS in an online supplement. Finally, we provide a real data example to highlight the unique inferences that can be drawn with our approach. The goal of this tutorial is to equip researchers with the necessary tools to apply advanced multilevel models of cognitive change and retest learning in high-frequency assessment designs.

articles.title: Widely Used, Unevenly Evaluated? Generative AI Use, AI-Output Evaluation, and Their Association with Socioeconomic Background Across 59 Countries (PISA 2025)
articles.authors: Eileen Richter; Sebastian Röhl; Joshua Weidlich; Luisa Köhler; Ada Jung; Korbinian Moeller; Markus Spitzer
articles.abstract: Generative AI chatbots have become part of 15-year-olds' schoolwork. However, it is less clear whether these students also evaluate what these systems produce. Using PISA 2025 data from more than 500,000 students across 59 countries, we examined how often students are asked in class to evaluate AI output, who is asked, and how closely the practice is associated with students' AI use. On average across countries, 57.5% of students used AI chatbots for schoolwork at least weekly, yet only 35.3% reported being asked often or very often to evaluate the quality of AI output in class, whereas 33.2% reported being asked never or almost never. Interestingly, students who used AI more often also reported being asked more often to evaluate AI output, in all countries (pooled r = 0.34). Yet, 25% of at-least-weekly users still reported no or almost no AI-output evaluation. Furthermore, students from more advantaged socioeconomic backgrounds reported being asked more often to evaluate AI output, independent of their level of AI use. Overall, students reported being asked to evaluate AI output less often than to evaluate online information. Yet, the association of AI use with evaluation was substantially stronger for AI-output than for online-information evaluation. In sum, many students who use AI regularly report few opportunities to evaluate its output in lessons, and these opportunities are socially stratified, extending an established pattern of digital inequality to generative AI.

articles.title: Decoding Affect: A Computational Model of Affective Adaptation and Construction
articles.authors: Haijiao Cui; Liu-Fang Zhou
articles.abstract: Affective construction and adaptation are complementary processes through which affective value is generated and evolves over time. Although prior research has identified key determinants of these processes, including reference points, stimulus inherent value, attention, negativity bias, adaptation rate, and time, a unified framework that quantifies how these factors interact and jointly shape affect remains lacking, leaving important nonlinear affective phenomena insufficiently explained. We propose the Attention-Reference Interaction Adaptation (ARIA) framework, which formalizes affective valuation as an attention-gated dual-reference integration process that evaluates current sensory inputs relative to both prior experience and allostatic set-points. By specifying how value salience and negativity bias jointly govern attention allocation and adaptation rate, ARIA suggests that relativity and asymmetry (two foundational properties of affective valuation) arise from a shared attentional mechanism. Consequently, these properties are contingent, dynamically coupled, and conditionally reducible, rather than fixed, independent, and irreducible axioms as assumed in classical behavioral economic theories. Furthermore, we map ARIA's computational components onto reward and interoceptive prediction errors, capturing how external and internal discrepancies jointly drive the construction of affective experience. Through numerical simulations and an initial empirical test, we show that ARIA reproduces classic affective phenomena, such as exponential decay, affective after-reactions, and alliesthesia, while also accounting for anomalous patterns, including cases in which environmental improvements fail to elicit pleasure and conditions under which inherently positive stimuli adapt more slowly than negative ones. Ultimately, ARIA offers a tractable computational framework for explaining affective dynamics and generating testable predictions about well-being and environmental experience.

articles.title: The Temporal Dynamics of Cognitive Control at Short and Long Timescales
articles.authors: Su Wang; Jacob Sellers; Han Zhang; Jahla Osborne; Taraz Lee; John Jonides
articles.abstract: Response-conflict tasks, such as the Simon and flanker tasks, are widely used to study how individuals exert cognitive control to override prepotent automatic responses (habits) in favor of goal-directed actions (goals). As task demands vary—from local, trial-by-trial interference to global changes in conflict frequency—control parameters may need to be adjusted to maintain task performance. Such cognitive control adaptations can be examined through congruency sequence effects (CSE, the congruency effect is reduced following an incongruent trial compared to a congruent trial) and list-wide proportional congruency effects (LWPCE, the congruency effect is reduced in mostly incongruent compared to mostly congruent blocks). Although both effects involve adjustments in control, it remains unclear whether these adjustments reflect similar or different mechanisms. Here, we used a “forced-response” paradigm combined with a computational model to understand the temporal dynamics of cognitive control that contribute to CSE and LWPCE. This approach allowed us to decompose cognitive control into the latencies of habitual and goal-directed processing and the probabilities with which these processes are expressed as overt behavior. We found that both recent conflict (driving the CSE) and frequent conflict within a block (driving the LWPCE) accelerated goal-directed processing and—in the Simon task only—increased the likelihood of inhibiting the habitual output; the LWPCE persisted after accounting for previous-trial congruency and thus could not be fully reduced to an accumulation of the CSE. These findings indicate that cognitive control adaptations share a common computational signature when regulating conflicts at both short and long timescales.

articles.title: Shape is a good cue, not a ubiquitous one: lexical statistics of early nouns in English and Korean
articles.authors: Samah Abdelrahim; Jongmin Jung; Eon-Suk Ko; Michael C. Frank
articles.abstract: The shape bias, children's tendency to generalize new words by shape, is well documented in English-speaking children and reportedly weaker in children acquiring typologically different languages such as East Asian languages. One prominent explanation for the shape bias, the statistical generalization account, attributes the bias to the distributional dominance of shape-organized nouns in the early lexicon. We investigated this hypothesis, asking English and Korean adults to rate early-acquired common nouns. Most nouns were rated as solid and countable. In English speakers' ratings, far fewer were rated by shape than the account predicts, shape was chosen less often than material, and there were no detectable differences in the distribution of shape ratings across 16 languages' unilemma sets. Korean adults did not rate nouns as less shape-organized than English adults, contrary to what the weaker shape bias reported for East Asian language-speaking children would predict. Procedural differences had a large effect on the rate of shape organization. Despite these results, higher shape ratings were associated with earlier average age of acquisition, while solidity and countability, which are far more common, did not add unique predictive value in the pooled English-rated model. These findings suggest that shape may be a good cue for early noun learning, but not a ubiquitous or distinctively informative one relative to others, and that distributional differences may not be the key locus for cross-linguistic variation.

articles.title: Metaphorical cost: Processing of metaphorical and literal language in people with Alzheimer’s disease
articles.authors: JAN EDSON RODRIGUES LEITE
articles.abstract: Whether metaphorical language is processed differently from literal language remains an open question: lesion and imaging studies have pointed to partly distinct neural substrates, whereas reading-time studies have found comparable costs when context is supportive. This study examines the question in speakers of Brazilian Portuguese with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), a condition that affects both semantic and visuospatial abilities, and asks whether the conceptual content of a sentence, spatial or non-spatial, modulates processing cost independently of metaphoricity. Forty-two participants (14 with AD, 14 healthy elderly and 14 healthy young adults) read twelve sentences in a 2 × 2 design (metaphorical or literal; spatial or non-spatial) on a tablet and judged an inference about each of them. Accuracy, reading times and response times were recorded. The AD group was less accurate and slower overall. Spatial sentences were read more slowly by all groups. Metaphoricity interacted with group in reading times: only the AD group read metaphors more slowly than literal sentences, and this cost was concentrated in metaphors with a spatial source domain. Spatiality interacted with group in response times, although comparisons within groups were not significant. The results indicate that the cost attributed to metaphor depends on the population tested, on the stage of processing that is measured and on the conceptual domain recruited by the sentence. They do not support a general processing disadvantage for metaphorical language.

articles.title: Actual use of generative AI chatbots for mental health advice across adulthood: Psychological correlates and the moderating role of age
articles.authors: Angeliki Triantafillaki; Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Parisis Gallos; Ioannis Moisoglou; Panagiota Peleka; Petros Galanis
articles.abstract: Little is known about which adults actually turn to generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for mental health advice, and whether the profile of these users changes with age. The aim of this study was to examine the sociodemographic and psychological correlates of actual chatbot consultation for mental health advice, and of its frequency. In this cross-sectional online survey, 843 Greek adults aged 18 to 50 years reported whether, and how often, they had consulted an AI chatbot about their thoughts and feelings during the previous three months. Validated instruments captured anxiety, depression, loneliness, sleep quality, self-esteem and problematic social media use. Logistic and proportional odds models, extended with age-by-predictor product terms, were fitted. Seven in ten respondents (71.3%) reported such use, and 37.5% did so weekly or more often. Independent correlates of any use were younger age, recent consultation with a mental health professional, greater problematic social media use and lower self-esteem. Among users, worse sleep, lower self-esteem and greater problematic social media use were associated with more frequent consultation of AI chatbots for mental health advice. Age moderated the role of loneliness, which was related to chatbot use only among the youngest respondents, and a comparable but weaker gradient emerged for depressive symptoms. Chatbot-based mental health advice is now widespread among Greek adults up to midlife. Clinicians should ask patients of every age about it, and preventive efforts should recognize that its psychological drivers are not uniform across adulthood.

articles.title: Gender and Agency in AI Career Guidance for Women: A Socio-Technical Audit of General-Purpose Language Models
articles.authors: Sara Portell Fonolla; Yasmina El Fassi
articles.abstract: People ask general-purpose chatbots for advice on personal decisions, including their careers. Studies of gender bias in large language model (LLM) career advice mostly score single outputs about a person described to the model. But career guidance is a conversation with the woman herself, in which the advice can end up making the decision for her or treat a barrier she faces as a lack of confidence. We report a preregistered socio-technical audit of the career guidance that ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude give women through their APIs. We scripted 34 multi-turn conversations grounded in research on women’s careers, ran each five times per system, and added male versions of 14 to test gender cues (972 conversations). Human raters scored 304 conversations on nine objectives drawn from that research and from coaching ethics, with a second rater and an expert adjudicator for disagreements. Failures to preserve her agency had the highest share for every system (36% to 50% of conversations scored 1 or above on a 0 to 3 scale) and were more frequent than gender bias failures. Gemini was more often sycophantic. Swapping the user's gender showed no systematic difference, but pair differences depended on how the name was given. No LLM judge agreed acceptably with human raters, and the human raters also often disagreed, so the rates are descriptive. Audits of AI career advice should use more than one gender cue and, because models change, be repeated over time. LLM judges can serve as a screening aid, but scoring needs two or more human experts.

articles.title: What the Tally Hid: Screening Live-Observation Codes for Saturation, Floor Effects, and Degeneracy Before Piloting
articles.authors: Vince Jacques de Blauwe; Antonio Fidalgo
articles.abstract: Observational coding instruments are usually judged by their summary score, yet a well-distributed total can hide codes that cannot discriminate between units. We set out a pre-piloting screening protocol for live-observation coding sheets and calibrate it on a worked case. In 15 stranger dyads, a ten-code sheet produced a healthy-looking composite (M = 26.63, SD = 9.64), yet four engagement codes ran at 74–94% of their protocol maximum, three withdrawal codes sat at 0–8%, and only three codes varied in a graded way between dyads. Resampling the deposited counts, the all-code conjunctive rule detected this pattern in 100% of pilots from N = 2 to 15, but against a no-pathology null it raised false alarms in 33.1% of pilots at N = 2 and 9.2% at N = 4, falling below 5% only from N = 6. Excluding the never-observed monologue and silence codes, detection was flat and non-monotonic (90.8% at N = 4; 87.0% at N = 6). Threshold distance and code degeneracy, not pilot size, govern whether screening succeeds. We therefore recommend reporting each code’s percentage of maximum, between-unit variance and signed distance to the nearest threshold, rather than a pilot N. A closed-form margin index built from these quantities, z = d√N/SD, reproduced the simulated code-level results to within 1.2 percentage points on average from N = 4 and is released as an R function. The protocol and its two principles are provisional and unregistered, pending replication on a second bin-level dataset; all counts come from a single non-blinded coder.

articles.title: People will buy non-cooperative rules
articles.authors: Connie Pui Yee Chiu; Ana Gantman
articles.abstract: Institutional rules enable large-scale human coordination, allowing strangers to cooperate by adhering to official rules that apply to all. Yet not all rules serve these cooperative ends. Why do they persist? Across three pre-registered experiments in the United States and China (N = 1610) players could buy rules in a Dictator Game. Even when the rules available for purchase did not serve cooperative ends, nearly half of U.S. participants (Study 1) and two-thirds of the Chinese participants (Study 2) bought at least one rule—more than the 33% that a separate sample of Americans forecasted would be willing to pay, and despite judging them to be of little utility. Both preferences for obedience (in the United States and China) and support for anti-democratic practices (United States) predicted “non-cooperative” rule purchasing, a phenomenon specific to non-cooperative rules as preferences for obedience predicted buying “non-cooperative” but not cooperative rules (Study 3).

articles.title: EEG and self-report reveal preserved explicit appraisal of others’ pain but reduced modulation of affective and sensorimotor responses in autistic adults
articles.authors: Igor Riečanský; Ekaterina Pronizius; Martin Marko; Milan Mitka; Andreas de Lorenzo; Claus Lamm
articles.abstract: Empathy for pain—sharing another person’s affective state while maintaining self–other distinction—triggers sensorimotor and cognitive-emotional responses in the observer. We investigated whether these processes differ in autistic adults (ASD) and non-autistic controls (CON). Twenty ASD and 21 matched CON viewed images of a hand being either gently touched with a cotton bud or injected with a needle. For injection trials, participants were informed whether the target could feel pain (pain-sensitive) or not (pain-insensitive, due to local anesthesia), allowing assessment of how cognitive appraisal of the target’s pain sensitivity contributes to the empathic responses and their context-dependent modulation. EEG recorded sensorimotor engagement via event-related desynchronization (ERD) of central mu (7–13 Hz) and beta (14–25 Hz) rhythms. Participants also rated the target’s pain and their own unpleasantness. Both groups rated pain-sensitive injections as more painful than pain-insensitive injections, with no group differences, indicating comparable explicit appraisal of others’ pain in ASD and CON. In contrast, self-reported unpleasantness and ERD were modulated by target pain sensitivity only in CON, who reported greater unpleasantness and stronger mu ERD when the target could feel pain vs. not; this modulation was absent in ASD. No group differences emerged for touch or pain-insensitive injections, and viewing perspective (egocentric vs. altercentric) did not differentially affect responses. These findings suggest preserved explicit appraisal of others’ pain in autistic adults but reduced contextdependent modulation of affective and sensorimotor responses, pointing to a selective alteration in affective and sensorimotor sharing rather than a global empathy impairment in ASD.

articles.title: Inward-directed utterances and the evolution of language
articles.authors: Conor Houghton
articles.abstract: At some point in our evolutionary history humans gained the ability to communicate using language. Most accounts of language evolution focus on its role in communication. This review proposes an alternative: that the decisive step was the internalisation of utterance as a tool for directing thought. A hierarchy of animal communication is developed to sharpen this proposal. Evidence from the development of language in children supports the view that internalisation is central to language acquisition. The success of chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models provides a further, independent demonstration of the importance of language as a tool. These proposals together suggest that language is patterned on the structure of thought rather than shaped primarily by the demands of communication.

articles.title: Moral Preferences Theory of Redistribution
articles.authors: Elijah Paul Galvan; Alan Sanfey
articles.abstract: In recent years, the steady rise of economic inequality across the globe has accompanied an ever-increasing focus on the question of redistribution. Though the majority of people believe that economic inequality is a problem, policy decisions to redistribute resources are typically highly contentious. Previous psychological, sociological, and political science theories which attempt to explain the paradox between stated beliefs and actual behavior in redistributive choice have largely relied upon an unverified assumption that redistributive preferences are derived from perceptions about pre-existing inequality. Here, we propose a Moral Preferences Theory of Redistribution, which integrates intuitions and prior research derived from various modeling frameworks across psychology, cognitive neuroscience, and economics. This theory posits that that redistributive behavior is guided by multiple moral principles, and that the preferences that guide the selection of these principles are both context-dependent and reflect dispositional individual values. This theory was tested using a multi-methodological approach: across two experiments – a large behavioral experiment (N = 231) and a direct fMRI follow-up study (N = 50) – the data show converging evidence to support the Moral Preferences Theory across multiple levels of analysis: political, psychometric, computational, and neural.

articles.title: “The Reports of My Death Are Greatly Exaggerated”: Humans Can Extract Unconscious Bigram Knowledge in the Artificial Grammar Learning Task
articles.authors: Andrei Preda; Andrei Razvan Costea; Adrian Opre; Răzvan Juchiș
articles.abstract: Humans often appear to possess knowledge they cannot fully articulate. For instance, in the landmark artificial grammar learning (AGL) task, participants acquire knowledge of a complex regularity (grammar) that structures letter sequences, while typically claiming to have little or no subjective access to the regularity, suggesting that learning has been largely unconscious. A highly influential argument against this conclusion comes from studies showing that participants can identify simple letter pairs (bigrams) that the grammar is composed of when asked to do so. Consequently, the unconscious status of learning in AGL has remained highly controversial. Crucially, however, these latter studies have never measured participants’ subjective states when performing the bigram identifications but have assumed that bigram identification necessarily reveals conscious knowledge. In this paper, we test this critical assumption by employing novel bigram-based artificial grammars and, simultaneously, by measuring participants’ subjective access to their bigram knowledge. For generalization, we employed both typical letter stimuli and face stimuli. Participants (N = 188) memorized strings (of faces or letters) constructed from the grammars; subsequently, they classified novel strings (half grammatical, half nongrammatical), reporting subjective awareness trial-by-trial. We found that letter strings were classified above chance based both on unconscious and on conscious knowledge (all ps < .001, Bayes factors > 10⁷), while data were insensitive for the faces condition (Bayes factors between 0.33 and 3). Our findings demonstrate unconscious learning of bigrams for letter strings, challenging the influential idea that accurate bigram knowledge necessarily reveals conscious knowledge.

articles.title: Examining HiTOP Through Naturalistic Symptom Descriptions in Anonymous Online Mental Health Forums: A Mixed-Methods Study Protocol
articles.authors: Drin Ferizaj
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Background: The Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) organises covarying symptoms and maladaptive traits into transdiagnostic dimensions to address limitations of categorical diagnosis. Naturalistic symptom descriptions may complement structured assessments. Objective: This protocol describes a reproducible mixed-methods workflow to derive symptom indicators from forum posts and examine their organisation relative to HiTOP. Methods and analysis: The target sample is 80,000 public Reddit posts. After local de-identification, a large language model (LLM) will extract symptom labels and supporting paraphrases. Two human experts will independently review outputs for up to 250 posts. Three embedding models will flag potentially equivalent symptom labels for local LLM assessment. Two experts will qualitatively review the most frequent canonical symptom labels (at least 1,000) and develop a codebook of symptom categories, continuing until a prespecified saturation criterion is met. An LLM will assign canonical symptom labels to these categories, producing binary post-level indicators. Multiverse-inspired structural analyses will compare network, component, factor, and clustering representations across discovery, internal tuning, and holdout partitions. Evaluation will assess interpretability, stability, and agreement with expert mapping to HiTOP. Supplementary analyses will include agent-assisted exploration, codebook application to DepressionEmo and the Reddit Mental Health Dataset, and pooled integrative analysis that may include additional comparable corpora.
Discussion: The study will examine whether symptom co-expression within posts forms interpretable patterns corresponding to HiTOP.
Ethics: The Ethics Committee of Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin approved the study (EA2/274/25). The study was preregistered on 8 May 2026 (German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS00040244).
Keywords: Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology, natural language processing, large language models, Reddit, mixed methods, study protocol

articles.title: Characterizing deaf and hard-of-hearing language experiences as arousal-regulation processes
articles.authors: Christina Kim; Laurel Aichler; Onudeah Nicolarakis; Shilpa Hanumantha Lacy; Rachel Sortino; Rachel Pizzie
articles.abstract: Empirical language research with deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) groups often includes proficiency, age of acquisition, or language background measures but excludes people’s socioemotional context. Measuring socioemotional context depends on characterizing the socioemotional experiences associated with DHH language development and use. We used the biopsychosocial model of arousal regulation as a theoretical lens to explore 11 qualitative interviews with DHH participants. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we developed three characteristic themes: 1) Deafness is not a monolith, 2) Name it to tame it – Language Anxiety, and 3) Positive roots for resilient shoots. These themes show that DHH language experiences are heterogeneous, that negative experiences can represent language anxiety, and that positive experiences modulate arousal regulation. Our study highlights new socioemotional considerations for language processing research like how emotions influence language use, how motivations support language skills, and how communication strategies impact social interactions within DHH communities.

articles.title: Subjective and objective socioeconomic status as predictors of midlife cognition in the rural Deep South: the Bogalusa Heart Study
articles.authors: Jade E. Jenkins; Amy Thierry; Ileana De Anda-Duran; Shakira Suglia; Lydia Bazzano; Owen Carmichael
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Lifecourse socioeconomic conditions influence Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) risk. Higher objective socioeconomic status (O-SES) is consistently associated with better later life cognition and lower ADRD risk. One’s perception of their socioeconomic status, or subjective socioeconomic status (S-SES), is a robust predictor of myriad health outcomes. However, it’s utility as a predictor of cognition in aging populations is not well characterized and has yet to be investigated in the Deep South, a historically underrepresented region characterized by socioeconomic disadvantage and elevated ADRD risk. 
METHODS: O-SES and S-SES were examined as predictors of cognition in the Bogalusa Heart Study. We derived O-SES using confirmatory factor analysis and measured S-SES using the country ladder from the MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status. Exploratory analyses were conducted to test for potential effect measure modification by sex and race. 
RESULTS: O-SES, but not S-SES, was associated with cognition in the full sample. Exploratory analyses revealed a small positive association between S-SES and cognition only for White men, which was attenuated after accounting for O-SES. The relationship between O-SES and cognition was not modified by sex and race.
DISCUSSION: Our finding that higher O-SES is associated with better cognition is consistent with extensive evidence. However, we did not replicate previously found associations between S-SES and cognition observed in other older populations and with numerous other health outcomes. Given the paucity of research in the rural Deep South, more work is needed to understand S-SES and ADRD risk in this setting.

articles.title: Social media addiction is associated with poor mental health, AI chatbot use, and problematic digital behaviours among Generation Z: a cross-sectional study in Greece
articles.authors: Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Angeliki Triantafillaki; Panagiota Peleka; Parisis Gallos; Ioannis Moisoglou; Olga Galani; Maria Tsiachri; Petros Galanis
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE To examine the association between social media addiction and mental health among members of Generation Z in Greece. Moreover, we examined the association between social media addiction and social media-related behaviours. METHOD We conducted a web-based cross-sectional study with a convenience sample of 599 individuals aged 18 to 29 years. We measured social media addiction with the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale. Outcomes were anxiety, depression, loneliness, social media fatigue, sleep quality, life satisfaction, physician visits for mental health issues, artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot use for mental health issues, second-screen use, social media distraction, fear of missing out, and no-social-media phobia. We performed multivariable logistic regression analysis adjusting for sex, age, and financial status, and we examined interactions between social media addiction and these variables. RESULTS Overall, 56.6% of participants were addicted to social media. The prevalence of anxiety was 57.5% among addicted participants and 38.1% among non-addicted participants, while the prevalence of depression was 39.2% and 25.8%, respectively. After adjustment for confounders, social media addiction was associated with higher odds of anxiety, depression, loneliness, social media fatigue, poor sleep quality, life dissatisfaction, and AI chatbot use for mental health issues. Also, social media addiction was associated with higher odds of second-screen use, social media distraction, fear of missing out, and no-social-media phobia. Sex, age, and financial status did not substantially modify these associations. CONCLUSIONS Social media addiction is highly prevalent among Generation Z and is associated with several mental health problems and problematic digital behaviours. Interventions to prevent social media addiction and to facilitate access to professional mental health care among young people are needed.

articles.title: Covert control over the real-time dynamics of human interactions with Ducksoup
articles.authors: Pablo Arias Sarah; Guillaume Denis; Philippe schyns; Rachael Jack; Petter Johansson; Lars Hall; Jean-Julien Aucouturier
articles.abstract:
Uncovering how facial and vocal signals shape social interactions is difficult because researchers
cannot control how humans behave during free conversations. Here we demonstrate that recent
advances in AI-based transformation filters enable researchers to have covert experimental control
over the real-time dynamics of social interactions. We introduce Ducksoup, a scientific
videoconference platform that allows researchers to collect social interaction experiments online,
realistically transform participants' faces and voices in real time mid-conversation, record the
synchronized interactions and extract multimodal time series from recordings for analysis. In a
preregistered experiment (N = 64 participants), we replicate recent laboratory findings in a fully
online setup: artificially aligning participants’ smiles increased mutual enjoyment while remaining
undetected. The paradigm also revealed feedback effects on participants’ spontaneous facial, vocal
and verbal behavior. By combining the ecological validity of free interactions with experimental
control and scalable data collection, Ducksoup turns natural conversations into a causal
experimental paradigm for psychology and neuroscience.

articles.title: Recovery Capital, Structural Barriers, and Wellbeing Among Adults in Addiction Recovery: Findings from the Life in Recovery Survey in Spain
articles.authors: Lucas Serrano-Pastor; Sylvia Georgieva; Alfredo Zarco Alpuente; Ângela Maria Teixeira Leite; Paula Samper-Garcia; Jose-Antonio Giménez-Costa
articles.abstract:
Understanding how personal, social, and structural conditions shape recovery capital is important for explaining differences in addiction recovery and wellbeing. This study examined strengths and barriers during active addiction and recovery and their associations with addiction complexity, recovery trajectories, social and structural conditions, perceived change, and wellbeing. A cross-sectional national survey included 1,598 adults in recovery in Spain who completed the Spanish-adapted Life in Recovery survey and measures of social and living conditions, quality of life, and harmony in life. Analyses included paired t tests, correlations, group comparisons, and hierarchical regression models. Participants retrospectively reported substantially more strengths (mean difference = 4.23, d = 1.03) and fewer barriers (mean difference = -4.74, d = 1.33) in recovery than during active addiction. Strength growth and barrier reduction were modestly associated (r = -.29), supporting their interpretation as related but distinct dimensions of recovery capital. Higher strengths in recovery were associated with more consolidated self-identified recovery stages, earlier problem identification and recovery initiation, use of multiple recovery pathways, and greater satisfaction with social and living conditions (R² = .128). Barriers were more strongly patterned by structural conditions, including employment, housing, and perceived economic situation (R² = .070). Higher strengths, fewer current barriers, and greater perceived barrier reduction were associated with better quality of life (R² = .092) and harmony in life (R² = .097), while women reported lower wellbeing after adjustment. The findings support a contextual and multidimensional understanding of recovery capital and highlight the importance of strengthening personal and social resources while addressing persistent material and structural barriers in recovery-oriented care.
Keywords: Addiction Recovery; Recovery Capital; Structural Barriers; Wellbeing; Life in Recovery; Recovery-Oriented Care.

articles_hidden.title: Anhedonia and Emotional Processing of Past- and Future-Directed Mental Representations: Behavioral and Event-Related Potential Evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Pillny; Kai Härpfer; Hannes Per Carsten; Anja Riesel; Julia Klawohn; Tania Marie Lincoln
articles_hidden.abstract: Anhedonia may involve difficulties generating affective value from remembered and imagined positive experiences rather than a generalized reduction in immediate pleasure. However, its association with emotional processing across direct stimulus exposure, memory retrieval, and prospection, including the role of negative affect, remain unclear. This preregistered study examined neural and subjective emotional responses in 48 nonclinical adults with varying levels of anhedonia. Participants viewed positive, negative, and neutral images, recalled them, and imagined future experiences involving their content. During 4,000-ms trials, late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes were assessed from 400 to 4,000 ms, alongside subjective affect and imagery vividness ratings. Anhedonia was assessed using the Snaith–Hamilton Pleasure Scale. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between anhedonia and LPP amplitudes across valence conditions and time windows, as well as subjective ratings across valence conditions. During recall, higher anhedonia was associated with reduced positive–neutral LPP differentiation at 1,000–2,000 and 2,000–3,000 ms, alongside lower pleasantness ratings for positive memories. Valence-dependent LPP associations were not significant during encoding or prospection. These findings suggest that altered affective processing of positive memories may be relevant to anhedonia, alongside broader differences in emotional responding and the vividness of mental representations.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Initial Validation of a Brief, Transdiagnostic Measure of Conflict Resolution Difficulties and Ineffective Relational Strategies
articles_hidden.authors: Kasey Stanton; Nicholas J. Brewster; Kayla Michelle Brown; Helena Towne; Jack D Burke; Isabella Whitesides; Christina G McDonnell; Corinne Carlton; Holly Frances Levin-Aspenson
articles_hidden.abstract: Considerable research in recent decades has focused on developing measures assessing transdiagnostic dimensions, including measures that target dimensional symptoms rather than traditional diagnostic categories. Furthermore, a sizeable literature has focused on assessing social-cognitive vulnerabilities (e.g., experiential avoidance) thought to be linked to an array of symptoms and functioning difficulties, and a range of measures of transdiagnostic, social-cognitive vulnerabilities have been developed. However, few of them include item content directly assessing conflict resolution difficulties and ineffective interpersonal relational strategies, which also are linked to a range of psychopathology and are targeted in cognitive-behavioral and third-wave treatments. We address this gap in the transdiagnostic assessment literature by presenting initial validation data for a measure of ineffective interpersonal strategies across three studies and four samples of participants (N = 301 adults; N = 808 adults self-identifying a mental health diagnosis; N = 368 undergraduate students; N = 226 community adults). Analyses based on these samples spanned evaluation of participant perspectives on item face validity, quantitative examinations of internal structure, test-retest stability, and evaluating validity associations with a range of self-report and interview measures. Results collectively support the initial validation of an efficient interpersonal measure, the 6-item Transdiagnostic Ineffective Relational Strategies Scale (TIRSS), which is provided in appendix materials for free use for research purposes. We discuss future validation steps to build from this work, as well as ideas for sharpening interpersonal and transdiagnostic assessment research more broadly.

articles_hidden.title: Neural Correlates of Partner Comparisons and Their Links to Intimate Partner Aggression
articles_hidden.authors: Sydney Kavanaugh; Alexandra Martelli; Samuel James West; Emily Lasko; David Skylan Chester
articles_hidden.abstract: People frequently compare themselves to their intimate partners. These partner comparisons are critical for relationship maintenance, with powerful ramifications for intimate partner aggression (IPA) perpetration. However, little is known about the neural correlates of partner comparisons and their relation to IPA perpetration. To address this gap, 96 participants from 49 intimate partner dyads underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and completed a social comparison task, judging their own negative and positive traits against those of their partner and the average person. Participants then reported whether they had any history of IPA perpetration. Consistent with previous findings, participants reported having less negative and more positive traits than others. However, participants’ tendency to compare themselves favorably to others was attenuated for their partners. Partner (> average person) comparisons were linked to heightened activity in the mentalizing network (DMPFC, precuneus, TPJ) and DLPFC, particularly for negative traits. Such DLPFC/DMPFC activity during partner comparisons related to greater IPA perpetration for negative traits and lesser IPA perpetration for positive traits. These findings suggest that recruiting mentalizing and executive control networks during partner comparisons may be meaningfully linked to IPA perpetration, depending on trait valence.

articles_hidden.title: Regulating Self-Interest: The Effect of Anodal tDCS over the Right Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex in the Ultimatum Game
articles_hidden.authors: Haim Assor; Jonathan slater; Eliran Halali
articles_hidden.abstract: In many social situations, a conflict exists between self-interest and social considerations such as fairness and reciprocity. Previous research suggests that self-interested behavior is an automatic response, requiring cognitive control to be regulated. Consistent with this view, neuroeconomics findings implicate the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) in regulating self-interested behavior and implementing social preferences. Whereas prior neuromodulation studies have shown that inhibition or disruption of the rDLPFC increases self-interested behavior, studies examining the effects of enhancing rDLPFC activity have yielded inconsistent results. Moreover, it remains unclear whether such enhancement promotes responses to intentional unfairness alone or also to inequality per se. In the present study, we applied anodal transcranial direct-current stimulation (tDCS) over the rDLPFC to reexamine its causal role in regulating self-interested behavior among ultimatum game responders. In addition, we tested whether this manipulation promotes responses to both intentional unfairness and inequality resulting from an intention-free process. The results show that anodal stimulation increased rejection rates of unfair offers, regardless of whether they were proposed by a human partner or randomly generated by a computer. These findings suggest that rDLPFC activity supports the implementation of social preferences more broadly, promoting both reciprocal fairness and inequality aversion. When considered alongside prior findings demonstrating an opposite effect of anodal stimulation applied to an adjacent lateral prefrontal region using a similar paradigm, the results point to distinct and complementary roles of lateral prefrontal regions in managing the conflict between self-interest and social preferences. We discuss implications for dual-process accounts of social decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: Seeing Through the Lens: Divergent Thinking and the Evaluation of Creative Product Designs
articles_hidden.authors: Vania Ardelia; Maryam Shahbazi; Moritz Reis; Ahmed Moustafa; Radwa Khalil
articles_hidden.abstract: Evaluations of creative products reflect both product characteristics and evaluator attributes. It remains unclear whether the ability to generate original ideas shapes how people evaluate creative products made by others. In this preregistered study, 97 university students first completed the Gough Creative Personality Scale, the openness items of the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and a self-report item on cultural orientation. In random order, they then rated five iconic chair designs on the Creative Product Semantic Scale and completed an Alternative Uses Task with six everyday objects. The chair ratings yielded each chair's perceived originality and perceived functional quality, and a large language model scored the originality of the Alternative Uses Task responses. Divergent-thinking originality did not predict the evaluation of any chair after correction for multiple comparisons, and creative personality did not strengthen this association as predicted. Openness to experience was associated with more favorable ratings of all chairs, whereas cultural orientation, gender, hobbies, and study year were not. In exploratory analyses, the association between perceived originality and perceived functional quality varied across the five chairs. It was strongest for chairs of intermediate perceived originality, a pattern consistent with the most-advanced-yet-acceptable principle. Design features were not manipulated, so this pattern requires confirmation with larger, systematically varied sets of products. Overall, originality in idea generation was not associated with more favorable evaluations of creative products. Evaluator openness and the specific design were more closely related to these judgments.

articles_hidden.title: Differences in associative change between cues trained in compound are better explained by individual prediction errors than by relative certainty
articles_hidden.authors: Amin Jahani; Metin Üngör
articles_hidden.abstract: The present experiments investigated associative changes during compound training involving cues with different learning histories. In six human predictive-learning experiments using the compound-test procedure (Rescorla, 2000), participants learned about the effects of foods (cues) on inflammation (outcome) in a hypothetical patient. Each food could cause decreases in inflammation, increases in inflammation, or had no effect. Cues A and C were trained as excitatory, whereas cues B and D were trained to acquire inhibitory properties. Participants then received compound training in which A and B were presented together and followed by an outcome that should produce associative loss, followed by a final test in which outcome expectations were assessed for the test compounds AD and BC. The initial training designs were expected to produce greater relative certainty about A than B, with A generating a larger individual prediction error than B during the compound training. If cues generating larger individual prediction errors undergo greater associative change, AD should receive lower ratings than BC. Alternatively, if participants preferentially attribute the compound outcome to the less certain cue (theory protection), BC should receive lower ratings than AD. Overall, the compound-test results were more consistent with an individual prediction-error account: AD was rated lower than BC in Experiments 1, 2, 5, and 6. Experiment 3 showed the opposite pattern, consistent with theory protection, but this pattern was not replicated in Experiment 4. We discuss the implications of these findings for the roles of prediction error and certainty in associative learning.

articles_hidden.title: The State of Play: Methodological Reflections on Phenomenological Psychopathology
articles_hidden.authors: Jodie Louise Russell; Lucienne Spencer; Matthew Broome
articles_hidden.abstract: In this paper, we reflect on the position of the researcher within the field of phenomenological psychopathology and the ways they can overcome privilege and outsider status in order to more accurately and ethically grasp the structure of disorder experience from the perspective of the person living it. §1 discusses problems incorporating lived experience as well as its challenges within phenomenological psychopathology. §2 introduces the phenomenological notion of play in the work of Husserl and Fink. §3 elaborates on the political and ethical dimensions of play using the work of Lugones, and §4 then discusses how playfulness might be applied in health research to overcome the problems outlined in §1. §5 then gives examples of how play might be utilised within the methodology of phenomenological psychopathology. Overall, we suggest that both researchers and those with lived experience can engage in processes of understanding that can facilitate safe and inclusive interactions through the medium of play.

articles_hidden.title: Pupil Dynamics Track Preparatory Control and Selective Learning in Decision Making
articles_hidden.authors: Yifei Deng; Jonathon R. Howlett; Marcelo G Mattar
articles_hidden.abstract: A unifying theory of phasic pupil responses suggests that pupil diameter reflects information gain following an observation. However, it remains unclear whether pupil responses track information indiscriminately or selectively encode specific types of information, and whether this selectivity shifts across task phases. To address this, we developed a decision making task with information streams from three sources: control signals, decision-relevant stimuli, and decision-irrelevant stimuli. This design allowed us to dissociate pupillary responses to different forms of information gain (Shannon surprise and learning) across sources and phases. Analyzing pupillometry data from 30 participants, we found modulators of pupil responses shifted from perceptual surprise to policy-related learning over the course of trials. Furthermore, cue-related surprise drove responses immediately after its presentation and during perceptual processing of stimuli, whereas decision-relevant learning modulated responses only post-decision. These findings refine the information-theoretic framework by distinguishing automatic, surprise-related dilation from selective, learning-related dilation gated by decision relevance.

articles_hidden.title: Born on Rhythms: Mother–Foetus and -Infant Neurophysiology as a Dynamic System of Metastable Coupled Oscillators
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Ciaunica; Earl K. Miller; Shir Atzil; Antonio Criscuolo
articles_hidden.abstract: The human embryo grows within a pulsatile maternal milieu structured by cardiac, respiratory, locomotor, vocal and circadian rhythms.
