The PMFM introduces a structured generative model that connects hidden melodic structure to observed sound by incorporating physical force-like relations. Like statistical models, the PMFM casts melodic expectation as probabilistic inference in a generative model, but unlike statistical models, the PMFM's generative model does not require learning from corpora. Instead, it is structured around a small set of force-like relational rules that operate over continuous latent states. Probabilistic inference in this generative model enables predicting the last note of a melody from its beginning notes. The PMFM strongly correlates with human performance in an existing dataset of melodic predictions. Compared with established statistical models, the PMFM, despite not being trained on corpora, explains similar or more variance in human data, including additional unique variance not explained by these models. Our model suggests that, beyond statistical learning, melodic expectation is also shaped by an "intuitive physics" basis.

articles_hidden.title: Sequential Priming Builder: A Free, No-Code Tool  for Implementing Sequential Priming Paradigms
articles_hidden.authors: Yubo Zhou; Jiaxi Ye; Wen Song; Zihan Yang; Mo Han; Wenlu Du; Lu Zang; Xi Shen
articles_hidden.abstract: Sequential priming tasks are a family of methods widely used in psychology. However, implementing sequential priming tasks typically requires custom programming and deployment through third-party platforms. To address these challenges, we developed a free tool that requires no coding skills — the Sequential Priming Builder (SP-Builder: spbuilder.org). This tool uses a graphical user interface that enables researchers to easily build different types of sequential priming tasks, which can be integrated into the widely used online survey platform Qualtrics. We assessed the tool’s reliability and timing accuracy in online environments across two studies. In Study 1, we showed that it correctly presented the predefined stimulus sequence and accurately recorded elapsed time. We also evaluated the timing error of stimulus presentation under conditions where typical online participant interactions were simulated. We conducted Study 2 using a preregistered Affect Misattribution Procedure (AMP; N = 92), a widely used sequential priming task. We built the study with SP-Builder, and the results replicated the published findings.

articles_hidden.title: The Morality of Partiality: How Relationship Expectations Shape Moral Evaluations
articles_hidden.authors: Zuleykha Gasimova; Amiya Shelly Aggarwal; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Alexander C. Walker
articles_hidden.abstract: While impartiality is often regarded as a moral virtue, acting impartially can violate social expectations and relational obligations, creating tension between competing moral considerations. The present research (N = 2,353) examined how people evaluate partial and impartial actors who prioritized either a socially connected other (family member, friend, or community member) or a stranger in need. Across sacrificial dilemmas and more ecologically valid helping scenarios, partial actors were judged more moral and trustworthy than impartial actors. This preference was strongest when impartial actors failed to prioritize a close (family member or friend), rather than more distant (community member), social tie. Impartial actors were also perceived as less predictable and as fulfilling less of their relational obligations, with these perceptions predicting judgments of their moral character. In Experiment 4, participants themselves exhibited a preference for partiality, with most preferring to help a socially connected other over a stranger in greater need. This preference was stronger when decisions were described as publicly observable rather than anonymous, consistent with reputational concerns influencing helping decisions. Together, these findings suggest that everyday moral judgments reflect not only assessments of adherence to abstract ethical principles but also inferences about individuals’ reliability as long-term social partners.

articles_hidden.title: Body image in relation to ADHD and ADHD traits: A mixed-methods scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Phaedra Longhurst; Lauren Makin; Fidan Turk; Helena Lewis-Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Accumulating evidence suggests associations between ADHD, negative body image, and 
disordered eating; however, relatively little is known about how body image has been 
conceptualised, assessed, and experienced. This mixed-methods scoping review aimed to 
map and synthesise existing research examining body image in relation to ADHD and ADHD 
traits. Seven databases (Embase, CENTRAL, CINAHL, MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO, and 
Scopus) and two grey literature sources (PsyArXiv and ProQuest) were searched from 
inception to September 2026. Data were charted iteratively and synthesised descriptively 
and narratively. Twenty-seven studies (25 quantitative, two qualitative) published between 
1995 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. All studies were based in Westernised contexts, 
with most employing cross-sectional designs. ADHD was predominantly assessed using
symptom-based measures and/or diagnostic status, while body image was most commonly 
assessed using subscales of the Eating Disorder Inventory. Quantitative studies primarily 
examined associations between ADHD and negative body image, with some evidence of 
greater negative body image in ADHD. However, findings were inconsistent across studies, 
particularly following adjustment for covariates (e.g., co-occurring psychopathology). The 
literature predominantly adopted pathology-oriented conceptualisations of body image, with 
no studies examining positive body image and limited exploration of lived 
experiences. Further gaps were identified in methodological approaches, the 
conceptualisation and measurement of body image and ADHD, and the representation of 
diverse populations. Reliance on predominantly neurotypical-derived conceptualisations and 
measurement tools not validated among ADHD samples raises concerns about their 
validity. Future research should prioritise participatory approaches to advance an inclusive, 
neuro-affirming understanding of body image among the ADHD population.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological dimensions of wise reasoning
articles_hidden.authors: Veronica Diveica; Bri Susanna Darboh; Roni Setton; Gary R. Turner; R. Nathan Spreng
articles_hidden.abstract: Wise reasoning is an adaptive capacity associated with wellbeing and pro-sociality across the lifespan, yet why some individuals reason more wisely than others remains unclear. We examined factors associated with individual differences in wise reasoning across five major psychological domains, and tested whether these associations differ between younger and older adults. A sample of 179 younger and 161 older adults completed a performance-based measure of wise reasoning, two self-report measures of wisdom traits, and a comprehensive battery assessing autobiographical memory, crystallized and fluid cognition, personality, affect, and social functioning. Greater wise reasoning capacity was associated with the richness of autobiographical recollection, better crystallized cognition, greater openness to experience, and better emotion recognition, but not affective dispositions. Cognitive performance accounted for more variance in wise reasoning than any other psychological domain. A data-driven analysis further revealed that wise reasoning capacity is best characterized by a multivariate pattern of covarying factors spanning psychological domains. Although most associations were similar across age groups, some evidence of age-related moderation emerged, including stronger associations with autobiographical memory vividness among younger adults and openness to experience among older adults. The correlates of wise reasoning did not fully generalize to self-reported wisdom traits, which were associated primarily with self-reported personality and affective dispositions. These findings advance an integrated account of the psychological foundations of wise reasoning across adulthood, highlighting their multidimensional nature, relative stability across the adult lifespan, and the key roles of autobiographical memory and crystallized cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion dysregulation in everyday life among children with ADHD: A cross-cultural qualitative study of parents’ accounts in Belgium and China
articles_hidden.authors: Canmei Xu; Lisa B Thorell; Mariette Huizinga; Ruwen Liang; Dieter Baeyens
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotional dysregulation (ED) is frequently observed among children with ADHD, yet little is known about how it unfolds in everyday life, particularly across cultural contexts. This qualitative study examined ED in primary school-aged children with ADHD in a Western cultural context (Belgium) and an Eastern cultural context (China). We interviewed 20 parents in each country and analyzed the interviews using meta-theme analysis. Across both groups, the interview accounts reflected a recurring sequence captured by five interrelated themes: context-specific triggers, emotional overload, dysregulated emotional expression, relational impact, and perceived effects on children’s self-image over time. The groups’ accounts differed in some of the situations parents described as triggers and in how parents interpreted emotional episodes and their consequences. These findings suggest that assessment and support for children with ADHD should take into account how families in different cultural contexts identify emotional triggers and interpret emotional episodes and their consequences.

articles_hidden.title: Individual and environmental predictors of math anxiety in primary school children
articles_hidden.authors: Monika Szczygieł; Mateusz Hohol
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous meta-analyses have indicated that math anxiety (MA) is weakly to moderately and negatively related to math achievement, yet relatively few studies have simultaneously examined a range of predictors of MA and the proportion of variance in MA explained by these predictors. We investigated individual and environmental predictors of MA using multilevel regression models based on data from 166 fourth-grade primary school children in Poland. We tested four models, sequentially introducing sociodemographic factors (gender, age), math domain-specific variables (math achievement, intellectual helplessness in math), domain-general affective factors (general and test anxiety), domain-general cognitive variables (fluid intelligence, working memory), and family-related factors (mothers’ home numeracy activities, MA, and education), while controlling for school as a fixed effect and including class as a random effect. Test anxiety was a stable predictor of MA across successive regression models. Intellectual helplessness in math and fluid intelligence were associated with MA in some models, but these predictors were not stable across successive models. The fixed effects, including school, explained approximately 58–63% of the variance in MA, while differences between classes accounted for only 1.4–2.4% of the variance. These findings underscore the need to consider both individual and environmental factors when developing interventions aimed at reducing MA and fostering a supportive learning environment.

articles_hidden.title: The cortical representation of materials and their properties
articles_hidden.authors: Hua-Chun Sun; Martin N Hebart; Filipp Schmidt; Roland Fleming
articles_hidden.abstract: Perceiving materials like metal, wood or soil is essential for many everyday tasks, yet we still understand little about how materials are represented in the brain. Here we report the most comprehensive mapping of neural representations of materials and their properties to date. In an event-related fMRI design over multiple sessions, six participants viewed every image in the STUFF dataset—which includes 200 different material categories—14 times each, yielding precise estimates of cortical responses. We compared these responses with 36 ‘core dimensions’ of material perception derived from >1.8 million perceptual similarity judgments on the same image set. This revealed ‘cortical feature maps’ of activity associated with each dimension. Most maps spanned large swaths of cortex, indicating a highly distributed and multiplexed representation. Multidimensional scaling revealed systematic relationships between the maps, with >95% of the variance between maps accounted for by just six axes. Despite this, for 35 of the 36 core dimensions, feature values could be decoded from brain activity patterns, and in pairwise comparisons, material categories could be decoded with 88.9% accuracy. Together our findings reveal a highly distributed multidimensional material representation that supports the read-out of both properties and categories of materials.

articles_hidden.title: How to Measure Victimhood and Moral Judgment with the Theory of Dyadic Morality
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Kubin; Kurt Gray
articles_hidden.abstract: The Theory of Dyadic Morality (TDM) argues that moral condemnation revolves around intuitive perceptions of victimization. We provide a curated collection of items for measuring moral judgment and perceived victimization, organized around one question: “From someone’s perspective, who is victimizing whom, how, and to what extent?” Each part of the question connects to a core element of our moral psychology, including the dyad itself (an intentional agent causing damage to a vulnerable victim), the continuum of perceived victimization (mild to severe), different kinds of victimization (e.g., physical violence versus spiritual suffering), and the important worldviews that shape perceived victimization (e.g., cultural and politics). We show how classic paradigms, from moral dilemmas to moral dumbfounding, can be measured with TDM, and we outline future directions, including how TDM can align artificial intelligence with human moral judgment.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Distance between Geographic Regions is associated with Lower Mobility, Weaker Democracy, and Increased Risk of Civil Conflict
articles_hidden.authors: Cindel J. M. White; Michael Muthukrishna
articles_hidden.abstract: Stable nations require strangers to coordinate and cooperate despite cultural differences. Using the Cultural Fixation Index (CFST) on World Values Survey data (268,992 participants; 95 countries; 2005–2022), we quantify cultural distances between demographic groups within countries, including between regions, ethnicities, religious groups, education levels, and social classes. We test whether within-country cultural distances are associated with national indicators of social mobility, democracy, and civil conflict. A pre-registered multiverse analysis (54,600 model specifications; 100 model families; 6 demographic groupings; 6 outcome measures) shows that only cultural distance between geographic regions is associated robustly with institutional weaknesses, such as higher corruption, weaker democracy, lower social mobility, and greater risk of civil conflict. In contrast, distances between ethnic, religious, and socioeconomic groups show few significant associations with national indicators of governance, mobility, and conflict, and educational distance is often associated with lower corruption and stronger democracies. The results imply that what matters is not diversity per se, but whether culturally distinct groups are geographically segregated.

articles_hidden.title: Reward sensitivity is associated with gambling participation, and financial vulnerability with problem gambling in U.S. adults
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: The rapid expansion of legal and online gambling in the United States has renewed public-health concern about gambling participation and gambling-related problems. These outcomes may have partly distinct correlates, yet they are rarely examined together within a single sample. We therefore tested whether demographic, contextual, financial, and psychological factors differentiated non-gamblers, recreational gamblers, and participants classified as problem gamblers. A nationally recruited, cross-sectional sample of 726 U.S. adults aged 18–80 completed measures of gambling behavior and symptoms, socioeconomic and financial vulnerability, mental health, loneliness, risk-taking, reward sensitivity, and neighborhood conditions. After adjustment for age and gender, reward sensitivity differed across all three groups, with the lowest scores among non-gamblers and the highest among problem gamblers. In adjusted models, reward sensitivity distinguished gamblers from non-gamblers. Among gamblers, socioeconomic deprivation and financial-exploitation vulnerability distinguished problem from recreational gambling, whereas reward sensitivity did not. In exploratory analyses, financial-exploitation vulnerability was more strongly associated with symptom severity among problem gamblers than among recreational gamblers after correction for multiple comparisons. Evidence for a similar group difference in socioeconomic deprivation depended on the scoring method. Reward sensitivity was positively associated with symptom severity at both low and high loneliness, with a stronger association at high loneliness. These findings suggest that gambling participation and problem gambling have partly distinct correlates: reward sensitivity distinguished gamblers from non-gamblers but not problem from recreational gamblers in fully adjusted models, whereas socioeconomic and financial vulnerability more clearly differentiated problem from recreational gambling.
